title: Graham v. Scissor-Tail, Inc.
summary: A powerful concert promoter could still be an adherent to an industry form; the arbitration requirement was expected, but selecting the other side’s union as arbitrator was unconscionable.
notes:
The famous phrase: the "minimum levels of integrity" required of a contractual arrangement for nonjudicial dispute resolution are not met by designating the union of one party as arbitrator, especially where the arrangement is the product of adhesion (Graham v. Scissor-Tail, Inc., 28 Cal.3d 807, 623 P.2d 165 (1981)).

The two-step California test for adhesion contracts stated in the opinion: enforcement is denied (1) if a provision falls outside the reasonable expectations of the weaker party, and (2) even if within those expectations, if the term is unduly oppressive or unconscionable.

The performer was Leon Russell, whose corporation Scissor-Tail, Inc. contracted with promoter Bill Graham.

sections.Parties: Bill Graham, a concert promoter, contracted with Scissor-Tail, the corporation representing musician Leon Russell. Their dispute concerned losses and profits from concert performances and the forum required to resolve that dispute.
sections.Material Facts:
Graham and Scissor-Tail entered four contracts in 1973 for concerts by Leon Russell on the American Federation of Musicians’ standard form. The form sent disputes to the union’s international executive board. The concerts had mixed results, and the parties disagreed about offsetting losses from one performance against profits from another.

Graham was commercially experienced and prominent. Nevertheless, major artists belonged to the union and its rules prevented them from signing a different contractual form. Graham had signed thousands of such agreements, including many with Scissor-Tail, and had participated in previous union arbitrations. His correspondence in the dispute even threatened to invoke that procedure. Thus the evidence of restricted choice differed from the evidence of notice: the form was effectively unavoidable, but its arbitration provision was familiar.
sections.Procedural History: Graham sued for breach. Scissor-Tail obtained arbitration, prevailed before the union board, and obtained confirmation of the award. Graham challenged the arrangement. The main excerpt finds the arbitrator provision unconscionable; the later assigned note at p. 705 explains that the court severed the objectionable selection provision and remanded for selection of a suitable arbitrator.
sections.Issue: Was this an adhesion contract despite Graham’s business sophistication, and did adhesion or unfairness prevent enforcement of the arbitration arrangement?
sections.Holding: The agreement was adhesive in this market. Adhesion alone did not invalidate it, and arbitration was within Graham’s reasonable expectations. The designation of the other side’s union as arbitrator was nevertheless unconscionable.
sections.Reasoning:
Bargaining power is relative to the transaction. Graham’s reputation did not give him a realistic alternative when artists of significance had to use the same union form. The court therefore evaluated whether the form or a particular term should be denied enforcement, rather than assuming that a successful businessperson necessarily negotiated it.

The court separated two inquiries. A term outside an adhering party’s reasonable expectations may be unenforceable, but Graham’s extensive experience defeated that particular objection. Independently, a term can be unduly oppressive even when fully expected. A dispute-resolution process controlled by the other side’s union failed the required minimum neutrality. The remedy preserved the agreement to arbitrate while removing the unacceptable arbitrator-selection mechanism. The case therefore separates assent, market choice, substantive fairness, and the remedy for an objectionable term.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Graham prevents two oversimplifications: sophistication does not establish bargaining freedom, and knowledge of a term does not establish its substantive enforceability.

topics.assent: Graham knew the arbitration term; informed expectations did not settle the separate fairness objection.
topics.adhesion: Industry-wide use of a mandatory form deprived even this experienced promoter of meaningful negotiating choice.
topics.unconscionability: A presumptively biased arbitrator made the selection provision unacceptable.
topics.arbitration: The court preserved arbitration through a suitable neutral rather than treating every arbitration agreement as invalid.
topics.severability: The later assigned note reports severance of the improper arbitrator provision.
topics.arbitration-formation: The case treats an arbitration clause's enforceability as a question of assent to an adhesion term plus unconscionability, and severs the arbitrator-selection provision rather than the arbitration agreement.

mnemonic.rationale: Bill Graham and the musicians’ union
